title: Thermal Paper 101 for Bakeries and Delis
description: How to choose the right thermal rolls and label printers for a bakery or deli — including BPA-free, food-safe, and moisture-resistant options that keep the line moving.
body:
Bakeries and delis print more tickets and labels than almost any other counter-service business: order tickets, scale labels, prep labels, shelf tags, and receipts. The wrong paper jams mid-rush, fades in a display case, or leaves residue on a printer head. The right paper keeps the counter moving and your labels legible. Here's what actually matters when you're choosing thermal paper for a bakery or deli.

How Thermal Paper Works (and Why It Matters for Food)

Thermal paper is coated with a heat-sensitive layer that darkens when the printer head applies heat — no ink or ribbon needed. That single detail drives most of the decisions you'll make: because the print is heat-triggered, it can also be triggered by a hot display case, a window with direct sun, or a heat lamp sitting too close to the label roll.

For food businesses, that means two things. First, choose a thermal grade that resists unintended darkening where you display or store items. Second, pay attention to how your labels and tickets hold up against moisture and grease — two constants in a bakery or deli.

Choosing the Right Rolls for Tickets and Receipts

Start with your printer, not the paper. Most counter-service printers specify an exact roll width and diameter, and a core size. Using a roll that's too wide or too thick causes jams; a roll with the wrong core simply won't seat. Check the model's spec sheet before you order.

  • Width and diameter: The two numbers printed on the inside of the receipt drawer or in the printer manual. Match them exactly.
  • Core size: Most 80mm receipts use a 12.7mm (half-inch) core, but 3-inch cores appear on label and scale printers. Getting this wrong is the most common ordering mistake we see.
  • Paper thickness: Measured in microns or GSM. Thicker paper costs a little more but is less likely to jam and feels more substantial in a customer's hand.

For bakeries and delis specifically, look for a top-coated thermal paper. Top-coating improves resistance to moisture and light oils — meaning a ticket handled with lightly greased hands or set on a damp counter stays legible longer.

Label Paper and Food-Safe Printing

Scale labels and prep labels have a different job than receipts. They need to stay stuck to waxed paper, deli wrap, clamshells, and containers that go into coolers or freezers.

  • Adhesive type: A general-purpose adhesive may lift off a cold or lightly oily surface. For refrigerated and frozen items, ask for a cold-temperature adhesive.
  • Moisture resistance: Labels in a cooler or on condensation-prone containers need a moisture-resistant face stock, or the text bleeds.
  • BPA-free options: Many bakeries and delis now ask for BPA-free thermal stock, and it's widely available for both receipts and labels. If it matters to your customers, it's worth specifying on the order.

One practical note: if your labels go directly on food-contact surfaces (rare but possible with some scale setups), confirm the stock is rated for direct food contact. Most bakery and deli labels go on packaging, not food itself — but it's worth verifying rather than assuming.

Storage: The Quiet Reason Labels Fail

Thermal paper degrades in heat, humidity, and light — all of which are abundant in a busy kitchen or behind a display counter. Store your rolls in a cool, dry spot, off the floor, away from ovens and windows, and use the oldest rolls first. A roll that has been sitting near a heat source may already be darkened before you load it.

If your labels are fading in the case or on the shelf, the culprit is usually storage or a display heat source — not the paper grade itself. Fix the environment first, then adjust the stock if the problem persists.

Conclusion

Thermal paper isn't a one-size-fits-all purchase for bakeries and delis. Match your rolls to your exact printer specs, choose a moisture-resistant top coat for receipts, and ask for cold-temperature adhesive and BPA-free stock on your labels. Store rolls cool and dry, and you'll cut most jams and faded labels before they happen.
